claim.pdf_says: a data item described with usage binary-char, binary-short, binary-long, binary-double, float-short, float-long, or float-extended, or of a standard floating-point usage; or
claim.markdown_says: — a data item described with usage binary**-**char, binary-short, binary-long, binary-double, float-short, float-long, or float-extended, or of a standard floating-point usage; or
claim.why_it_matters: Stray emphasis delimiters around the hyphen of 'binary-char' - an OCR/formatting artifact, not a transcription choice; the other six hyphenated usage names on the same line are plain. It renders as a bold hyphen and breaks literal grep for the reserved word 'binary-char'. No meaning is altered. Both occurrences are on page 595 (specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 24808 and 24816) and are the only two in the whole file.

verdict.reasoning: Independently confirmed against a 300dpi render of PDF page 595 (printed folio 565). GLYPHS AS PRINTED: in both bullet lists (general rules 2a and 2b) the line reads '- a data item described with usage binary-char, binary-short, binary-long, binary-double, float-' / 'short, float-long, or float-extended, or of a standard floating-point usage; or'. Every character of that sentence is set in the same regular roman face; the hyphen in 'binary-char' is a plain hyphen glyph, visually identical in weight, width and baseline to the hyphens in 'binary-short', 'binary-long', 'binary-double', 'float-long' and 'float-extended'. Nothing on the page body is bold - the only bold on page 595 is the running head 'ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)'. So the PDF has no emphasis on or around that hyphen, and the markdown's four '*' characters are absent from the source. Both quotations in the claim are accurate. The artifact is confined and correctly scoped: 'grep -o "[A-Za-z]\*\*-\*\*[A-Za-z]"' over the whole of specs/ISO_COBOL.md returns exactly two hits, both inside the page-595 section (the page-595 anchor is at line 24801, the next anchor follows). I checked the obvious false-positive routes and none applies: nothing is missing or reflowed away; there is no lost choice indicator; the markdown is not merely re-representing a line break. The one genuine line-wrap hyphen on these lines is in 'float-/short', and the transcription correctly rejoins it to 'float-short' - which proves the stray '**' is unrelated to hyphenation and is pure conversion noise. Bold is not a transcription convention for reserved words anywhere in this region of the file. I therefore rate this a real transcription defect rather than a formatting equivalence: the markdown carries characters the source does not, inside a reserved word, with no convention supporting them. Meaning is unaffected, so 'cosmetic' is the right severity, but the practical cost is real for this project - 'binary-char' appears 6 times in plain lowercase form elsewhere in the file (and 'BINARY-CHAR' 16 times uppercase), so these two occurrences are invisible to a literal reserved-word search of the spec.
verdict.corrected_description: CONFIRMED, with one correction to the line numbers. The stray emphasis delimiters are at specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 24811 and 24819, not 24808 and 24816 (the page-595 anchor is at line 24801). Everything else in the claim holds: the PDF prints 'binary-char' in plain roman with an ordinary hyphen identical to its six siblings on the same line, no bold appears anywhere in the page body, and these are the only two 'X**-**Y' occurrences in the entire file. Worth recording alongside it: the sentence really is hyphenated across a line break in the PDF, but at 'float-/short', which the transcription correctly rejoins - so the '**' pair is not a mis-handled line-break hyphen, it is unrelated conversion noise. Fix is to delete the four '*' characters on each of lines 24811 and 24819, restoring 'binary-char'.
